description: Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d) is a plaint-focused screening procedure. The court reads the whole plaint meaningfully, considers its material factual averments rather than the defendant's denials, and does not equate a prayer for relief with the facts constituting a cause of action.
conclusion_text: A Rule 11(a)/(d) challenge must be screened on the material factual allegations of the plaint as a whole, not by proving or disproving those allegations through the defence or by treating each requested relief as a separate cause of action.
jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court review of civil procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
source_quote: For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.

slots.name: rule11_challenge
slots.description: A party has invoked Rule 11(a) or (d) against the identified plaintiffs' plaint; recording the objection does not validate it.

slots.name: plaint_for_review
slots.description: An identified plaint, including its pleaded material facts and prayers, is the object of the screening; its allegations are not yet proven.

scope_limits: This rule prescribes the screening method; it does not find that a particular plaint actually discloses a sufficient cause of action.
A genuinely illusory or manifestly vexatious cause of action may still trigger Rule 11; the whole plaint, not an isolated paragraph, must be assessed.
Rule 11 does not allow rejection of only part of a plaint. Order VI Rule 16 striking out matter is a distinct mechanism.
Cited decisions are available only through this judgment's description of them.
unimplemented: The meaningful, whole-plaint appraisal of omitted material facts, illusory causes, and statutory bars is a semantic judicial evaluation, not an executable checklist.

description: A materially pleaded controversy over whether a trust's tenant relationship continued and how long the tenancy lasted is a civil tenancy subject, distinct from administering or investigating the trust under Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act.
conclusion_text: Where meaningful reading of the plaint identifies a substantive tenancy-continuance or tenancy-term controversy, those questions are for civil-court adjudication rather than determination as a Section 50 trust-affairs inquiry.
jurisdiction: India; Maharashtra trust-tenancy controversy under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as addressed by the Supreme Court
source_quote: The question of tenancy cannot be decided under Section 50 of the Act.

slots.name: plaint_screen_framework
slots.description: The screening must use the whole-plaint method produced by R1, not the truth of the trust's rebuttal.

slots.name: tenancy_dispute_characterization
slots.description: The target court characterizes the principal pleaded controversy as continuation and period of the tenancy; this is not a finding that an 11-year term, rather than an 11-month term, existed.

scope_limits: Only subject-matter suitability for civil tenancy adjudication is addressed; the tenancy's existence, duration, continuing validity, and plaintiffs' ultimate rights are not resolved.
The judgment says a tenant is not, by that status, a person having an interest in the trust for Section 51.
This does not independently decide every possible Section 80 objection or whether a different civil court is the proper forum.
unimplemented: Determining the true substantive subject of a plaint, rather than accepting nominal tenancy wording or clever drafting, remains an OPEN_TEXT assessment.
The competing alleged tenancy lengths and legal effect of any lease documentation are not adjudicated here.

description: A prayer to direct an inquiry into allegedly improper affairs of a public trust follows the distinct Section 50 trust-affairs route; the judgment describes prior Charity Commissioner consent under Section 51 for institution of a suit of the type specified in Section 50.
conclusion_text: A genuine trust-affairs inquiry prayer is treated under Section 50 and the applicable Section 51 consent regime rather than being converted into an ordinary tenancy question.
jurisdiction: India; Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as applied in the Maharashtra civil proceeding reviewed by the Supreme Court
source_quote: Such enquiries can only be undertaken under Section 50 of the Act.

slots.name: trust_affairs_prayer
slots.description: The plaint includes a separate prayer that the Commissioner inquire into alleged illegal acts by the trust and trustees; this records a requested remedy, not proof of illegal acts.

scope_limits: Section 51's prior-consent requirement is described for suits of the nature specified in Section 50; it is not imposed on every dispute with a trust.
The Commissioner who is asked to inquire is not the trust or its trustees, and the trust inquiry is not the same transaction as the tenancy.
The judgment does not supply proof of either a consent application or consent's absence, and it does not establish trust misconduct.
unimplemented: Whether a differently worded relief truly falls within Section 50, and any applicable consent facts, require case-specific examination.

description: Separation of pleaded material facts from requested reliefs prevents a trust-affairs prayer from automatically destroying the separate tenancy cause. Rule 11 cannot reject just one portion of a plaint, but a claimant who wants to relinquish some prayers must seek the appropriate order at trial, with Order II claim consequences kept distinct.
conclusion_text: When a whole-plaint review identifies a civil-adjudicable tenancy subject alongside a separate special-Act trust-inquiry prayer, the mere combination of those prayers does not itself justify rejecting the entire plaint; lawful restriction to tenancy issues and applications to relinquish other prayers are distinct procedural matters.
jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court review of Rule 11 rejection in a Maharashtra trust-tenancy civil suit
source_quote: Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed.

slots.name: holistic_gatekeeping
slots.description: Use R1's full-plaint, material-facts screening framework.

slots.name: civil_tenancy_track
slots.description: R2 has identified tenancy subject matter available for civil adjudication without deciding the tenant's merits.

slots.name: distinct_trust_inquiry_track
slots.description: R3 identifies the separate inquiry prayer; its transaction must remain distinct from the tenancy transaction.

scope_limits: This is a non-entailment rule: mixing prayers is not itself a sufficient Rule 11(a)/(d) ground. It does not immunize an otherwise defective plaint.
Only rejection of the whole plaint is tested here; partial rejection under Rule 11 is not authorized.
A relinquishment request must be addressed to the trial court under the applicable rules; Order II Rules 1 and 2 address claims omitted or intentionally relinquished.

The target court ultimately restricted adjudication to tenancy, tenancy terms and period, despite noting other civil-court-considerable prayers; this registry does not convert those prayers into granted relief.
unimplemented: The adequacy of the residual tenancy cause and any independent whole-plaint ground for rejection require the OPEN_TEXT appraisal from R2 and R1.
Whether and how other reliefs are legally relinquished requires a trial-court application; none is evidenced as completed by this judgment.

description: Opposing party assertions about an asserted eviction are recorded as opposing versions only. The presence of the two statements is different from establishing which account of possession is correct.
conclusion_text: The litigants advance contrary versions of the identified dispossession, without that record itself proving a forcible ouster, voluntary surrender by the same plaintiffs, or lawful taking of possession.
jurisdiction: India; evidentiary-role reconstruction of the Maharashtra civil plaint as reported in Supreme Court review
source_quote: This plea is strongly disputed by learned counsel for the respondent-trust who says that the possession was taken in accordance with law and as noted above, by voluntary surrendering by most of the tenants.

slots.name: claimants_ouster_allegation_recorded
slots.description: It is recorded that the plaintiffs alleged forcible eviction despite claimed continuing tenancy, without adopting the alleged event as a finding.

slots.name: trust_denial_recorded
slots.description: The trust disputes forcible dispossession and claims lawful taking; the stated surrender by most tenants cannot be attributed to any named plaintiff without identification.

scope_limits: TRUE applies to the recording of both assertions, not to the truth of either description of dispossession.
The judgment reports surrender by 22 of 44 tenants as a trust-counsel point; it does not identify the surrenders as the plaintiffs' acts.
The court notes controversy surrounding how long the trial court injunction operated; no chronology sufficient to resolve the merits is supplied.
unimplemented: No underlying possession documents, testimony, surrender instruments, or dates are independently available to establish whose account is accurate.

description: Continuation of an adjudicable tenancy issue is analytically separate from proving dispossession and from injunction discretion. The judgment describes Section 6 recovery for loss of settled possession without consent otherwise than by due course of law, but also recounts the rule that unlawful possession cannot be protected against the true owner by injunction; discretionary factors require separate assessment.
conclusion_text: Procedural survival of the tenancy issue cannot itself establish forcible dispossession, a right to Section 6 recovery, or entitlement to injunction; relevant evidence and discretionary injunction standards must be assessed separately in the appropriate trial proceedings.
jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court civil plaint-rejection review discussing Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and injunction principles
source_quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.

slots.name: surviving_tenancy_track
slots.description: R4's procedural non-rejection conclusion addresses the tenancy track, not possession relief.

slots.name: opposed_dispossession_versions
slots.description: R5 establishes that opposite accounts were asserted, not that either alleged event was proved.

slots.name: settled_possession_proof
slots.description: Whether the identified plaintiffs actually held settled rather than fugitive possession is not determined in this review.

slots.name: unlawful_dispossession_proof
slots.description: The plaintiffs' allegations and trust's contrary version conflict; the full nonconsensual and unlawful dispossession proposition is not decided. Timing relative to the trial injunction is material.

slots.name: injunction_discretion_merits
slots.description: Lawfulness of possession as against the true owner, prima facie case, balance of convenience, and any relevant conduct have not been decided as an injunction entitlement determination.

scope_limits: Section 6 restoration and discretionary injunction are different questions: possible recovery despite lack of title does not itself justify injunction against a true owner.

The judgment recounts a rule against injunction for a person in unlawful possession against the true owner, but does not find that these specific plaintiffs were unlawful possessors or that an injunction is due or barred on their merits.
The Supreme Court expressly leaves forcible-dispossession issues to the trial court if raised and relevant, and offers no view on the merits.
Claims about arrears, compliance with prior High Court orders, and surrender by other tenants are trust-side submissions or matters left for trial; their significance cannot be presumed.
The separate objection that only the District Court had jurisdiction was not specifically urged below and received no Supreme Court ruling.
unimplemented: OPEN_TEXT: evaluate settled possession, identity of the actual possessor, consent, lawful process, and the significance of possession dates and earlier injunction orders.
OPEN_TEXT: separately assess prima facie case, balance of convenience, true ownership, lawful or unlawful possession, the scope of discretion, and any relevant conduct.
No judgment-stage finding or supplied primary evidence resolves plaintiffs' claimed eviction; unknown and conflicted propositions cannot be promoted to either TRUE or FALSE by the procedural ruling.

description: Recorded procedural tenancy route and express reservation of merits do not decide those reserved merits.
conclusion_text: Continuation of the tenancy issue does not decide the reserved possession or injunction merits; a forcible-possession plea may be raised and considered only insofar as relevant to the continued suit.
jurisdiction: India; Supreme Court civil plaint-rejection review discussing Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and injunction principles
source_quote: The question of forcible possession as claimed is also a matter which can be pressed into service by the parties before the trial Court and if raised the Court shall deal with it considering its relevance to the suit and accept it or otherwise reject the plea in accordance with law. We do not think it necessary to express any opinion in that regard.

slots.name: surviving_tenancy_track
slots.description: R4's procedural non-rejection conclusion addresses the tenancy track, not possession relief.

slots.name: express_merits_reservation
slots.description: The court expressly declines a merits view and leaves a plea to trial only if raised and relevant.

scope_limits: Restricted to this judgment-stage reconstruction. Relevant pleas may be accepted or rejected; no mandatory full merits adjudication of every claim is inferred.
unimplemented: No independent assessment of possession, Section 6 relief or equitable injunction entitlement.
